Rules / Maintainability

SK7091 The process is terminated outside the entry point

Environment.Exit is called somewhere other than the entry point, so the process ends without unwinding.

CategoryMaintainability
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS1147

Why

Environment.Exit does not unwind. No finally runs, no using disposes, no buffered writer flushes and no await resumes. In a library, in a service, and in an executable's own helper class alike, it ends work that has nothing to do with whoever made the call — the caller's transaction is left open, its temporary file is left on disk, and its log line is left in a buffer that is never written.

Example

Instead of:

if (config is null) {
    Environment.Exit(1);
}

Write:

if (config is null) {
    throw new InvalidOperationException("no configuration was found");
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The rule does not try to tell an application from a library, and that is a measurement rather than a shrug. LooseLoader constructs its compilation with OutputKind.DynamicallyLinkedLibrary, so "this compilation is a library" and "no project file was loaded" are the same observation — and loose is the mode Skala exists for, because a folder of generated .cs files has no project. A rule keyed on OutputKind would report every console application analysed without its project file. The line drawn instead holds under every load mode: the entry point may end the process, because ending it is the process's own decision and there is nothing above to unwind into; everywhere else the call destroys cleanup somebody else wrote. The entry point is the compilation's own where there is one, and otherwise a static Main by name, which is the fallback loose mode needs. Top-level statements are the entry point and never fire. ⚠ Environment.FailFast is deliberately not reported: skipping cleanup is the whole point of it — it is what an author writes when the state is corrupt enough that running finally blocks is the more dangerous act — so reporting it would be reporting a decision rather than an accident. Environment.ExitCode is a property assignment, not a call, and never fires. The type is resolved by the semantic model and never matched on the written name. Report-only: the repair is to return, to throw, or to set an exit code and let the entry point end the process, and which of those the caller is owed is not something an edit can guess.
